Firstly, its P/E ratio of 25.7x is significantly higher than the sector benchmark of 18.01x [E6], indicating that investors are paying a premium for every rupee of earnings. This suggests that the stock may be overvalued relative to its peers. Secondly, the company's Price-to-Book (P/B) ratio stands at 3.76x, which is higher than the sector benchmark of 1.79x [E7]. This implies that investors are valuing DODLA’s assets more highly than what they represent in terms of book value. Moreover, despite its market capitalization of ₹6,065 Cr [E3], the stock currently sits at a discount to its intrinsic value as calculated by a discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis, which puts the intrinsic value at Rs 1335 per share against a market price of Rs 1009 [E42]. This leaves a margin of safety of 24.4% [E43], suggesting that the stock may be undervalued. However, it is important to note that DODLA's compounded profit growth over the trailing twelve months (TTM) has been negative at -4% [E19], which contradicts its positive fundamentals-led growth of 15% over five years and 28% over three years [E17]. This deceleration in earnings growth could be a red flag, as it suggests that the company may not be able to sustain its current profit margins. Additionally, DODLA trades at only 12% above its 52-week range low of ₹955 [E5], indicating that the stock is currently undervalued and has room for further appreciation. Despite this, the sector median profit growth rate is 16.3%, which suggests that DODLA may be trading below fair value.
